analogy.p: A **eukaryotic cell** is like a big library: the important books (DNA) are kept in a locked reading room (the nucleus) with a librarian controlling who gets access, and different rooms (organelles) do different jobs. A **prokaryotic cell** is like a single small room where the one important notebook (the DNA loop) sits on a table with everything else, with a few spare photocopied pages (plasmids) that can be handed to neighbours. The analogy breaks down because the DNA in a prokaryote is still organised and copied very accurately, so a bacterium is simpler but not "messy", and plasmid pages carry real genes, not photocopies of the main notebook.
analogy.t: A library and a pile of notes

bullets: **Eukaryotic cells** have a **cell membrane**, **cytoplasm** and **genetic material enclosed in a nucleus**.
**Prokaryotic cells** are **smaller** than eukaryotic cells and have **genetic material that is not enclosed in a nucleus**: a **single DNA loop** and **one or more plasmids**.
**Animal and plant cells are eukaryotic.** **Bacteria are prokaryotic.**
You must be able to describe how sub-cellular structures are related to their function (covered in detail in the next spec point).
You must be able to use the prefixes **centi, milli, micro and nano** and compare sizes (Higher tier: **standard form** and **order of magnitude**).
Typical marks: 1 to 2 marks for naming or labelling, 3 to 4 marks for a comparison, and 4 to 6 marks in a longer extended answer on cell types.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA expects you to **recognise, name and describe** the two basic types of cell, **eukaryotic** and **prokaryotic**, and to compare them. This is the starting point for the whole of cell biology, because every later topic (microscopy, mitosis, pathogens, genetic engineering) depends on knowing what is inside each type of cell. The examiners most often test it with a labelled diagram, a comparison question or a size calculation.

bullets: **Cell membrane**: surrounds the cell and controls which substances enter and leave.
**Cytoplasm**: a gel-like substance where most of the chemical reactions of the cell happen.
**Nucleus**: contains the **genetic material** (DNA, arranged in **chromosomes**) and controls the activities of the cell.
**Animal cells** are eukaryotic: they also have mitochondria and ribosomes.
**Plant cells** are eukaryotic: they have all of the above plus a **cell wall made of cellulose**, a **permanent vacuole** and, in green parts, **chloroplasts**.
Other eukaryotes include **fungi** (for example yeast) and many **protists**.
Human body cells contain **23 pairs of chromosomes** (46 in total) inside the nucleus.
Eukaryotic cells are typically **tens of micrometres** across, much bigger than bacteria.
core.p: A **eukaryotic cell** has its genetic material (DNA) kept inside a membrane-bound **nucleus**. The word comes from Greek roots meaning "true kernel", with the "kernel" being the nucleus. Eukaryotic cells also contain many other specialised **sub-cellular structures (organelles)**, each doing a particular job, which allows different chemical reactions to be carried out efficiently in different parts of the cell. Because these cells are generally larger and more complex, they are the cells that make up multicellular organisms.

bullets: **Cytoplasm**: contains the dissolved chemicals and the ribosomes where proteins are made.
**Cell membrane**: controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell.
**Cell wall**: surrounds the membrane and keeps the shape of the cell. The bacterial wall is made of a **different material from the cellulose** in plant cell walls.
**Single DNA loop**: the main genetic material, floating free in the cytoplasm (not in a nucleus).
**Plasmids**: small extra rings of DNA carrying additional genes.
**Ribosomes**: tiny structures where protein is made.
Some bacteria have a **flagellum** (a long whip-like tail) that spins to move the cell.
Bacteria have **no nucleus and no mitochondria**, but they still respire and make proteins.
core.p: A **prokaryotic cell** is a **much simpler and smaller** cell with **no nucleus**. Its genetic material is not enclosed in a nucleus but lies free in the cytoplasm as a **single, circular loop of DNA**. Alongside this main loop, the cell may have one or more **plasmids**, which are small extra rings of DNA. **Bacteria** are the prokaryotes you must know. Because there is no nucleus, there is no membrane separating the DNA from the rest of the cell contents.

bullets: If the **DNA is inside a nucleus**, the cell is **eukaryotic**.
If the **DNA is free in the cytoplasm** (a loop), the cell is **prokaryotic**.
A **prokaryote still has DNA**. It just is not enclosed in a nucleus.
Look for a **cell wall plus no nucleus** in a diagram: that is a bacterium.
Look for a **nucleus plus cell wall, vacuole and chloroplasts**: that is a plant cell.
Look for a **nucleus but no cell wall, vacuole or chloroplasts**: that is an animal cell.
Always state the **evidence from the diagram** when asked to identify a cell type: "it has no nucleus, so it is prokaryotic".
core.h: Why the nucleus is the dividing line
core.p: The names tell you the key difference. **Eu-karyote** means "true nucleus" and **pro-karyote** means "before nucleus", because prokaryotes appeared before cells with nuclei. The presence or absence of a nucleus is the single most reliable way to tell the two types apart in an exam. Everything else (size, complexity, number of organelles) follows from this. A nucleus lets a eukaryotic cell protect its large amount of DNA and control exactly which genes are used.

bullets: **Eukaryote**: DNA in **chromosomes**, **enclosed in a nucleus**, normally in **pairs** in body cells.
**Prokaryote**: **a single DNA loop**, **not enclosed in a nucleus**.
**Plasmids** are **extra** to the main DNA loop, not a replacement for it.
A bacterium can have **zero, one or many plasmids**.
Genes on plasmids are copied when the plasmid is copied, and the plasmid can be passed to other bacteria.
In both types, the DNA contains **genes** that code for **proteins**.
The loop of DNA is much **smaller** than the total DNA in a eukaryotic nucleus.
core.p: Both cell types store information as **DNA**, but the arrangement is different. In a eukaryote the DNA is packaged into several **chromosomes** inside the nucleus. In a prokaryote the main DNA is **one circular loop** lying in the cytoplasm. Prokaryotes can also have **plasmids**, which eukaryotic animal and plant cells do not normally have in the same way. The DNA carries the genes that code for the proteins the cell needs, so in both cases it controls the characteristics of the cell.

bullets: Plasmid = **small ring of DNA** found in bacteria.
Plasmids can carry **antibiotic-resistance genes** (link to Biology 4.3 on antibiotics and resistant strains such as MRSA).
Plasmids can be **transferred between bacteria**, spreading the genes.
Scientists use plasmids as **vectors** in **genetic engineering** to carry a new gene into a bacterial cell (link to Biology 4.6, Higher tier detail).
A plasmid is **not** a chromosome and **not** the main genetic material.
Plasmids are drawn as **small circles** separate from the main DNA loop.
They are much smaller than the main DNA loop.
core.p: A **plasmid** is a small, circular piece of DNA that is separate from the main DNA loop. Plasmids usually carry genes that are **not essential for everyday survival** but give a bacterium an advantage in some situations. The classic example is an **antibiotic-resistance gene**: a bacterium with this gene on a plasmid survives treatment with that antibiotic. Because bacteria can pass copies of plasmids to each other, resistance can spread through a bacterial population quickly.

bullets: Bacterium: roughly **1 to 5 µm** in length (give as "a few µm").
Animal and plant cells: roughly **10 to 100 µm**.
Prokaryotic cells are **smaller** than eukaryotic cells (this is the AQA wording).
Size is why a **light microscope** shows bacteria only as tiny shapes without internal detail.
Smaller size means a **large surface area to volume ratio**, so substances reach the middle of the cell by diffusion quickly.
To see detail such as plasmids you need an **electron microscope** (see microscopy notes).
Do not confuse **cell size** with the size of the **nucleus** or of organelles.
core.p: Prokaryotic cells are **smaller** than eukaryotic cells. Bacterial cells are often only a **few micrometres (µm)** long, whereas typical animal and plant cells are **tens of micrometres** across. This means a typical eukaryotic cell can be about **ten times larger** (about one order of magnitude) than a bacterium. Always make this a **comparative statement** (smaller than, larger than) rather than just saying "small".

bullets: The symbol for micrometre is **µm** (the Greek letter mu), not "um" or "mm".
To go from **mm to µm, multiply by 1000**: 0.5 mm = 500 µm.
To go from **µm to mm, divide by 1000**: 25 µm = 0.025 mm.
Check your answer makes sense: a cell in **metres** should be a tiny number.
core.p: You must be able to convert between units quickly and without errors, because cell sizes are tiny. The key idea is that each step between the units below is a **factor of 1000**. Converting down to a smaller unit makes the number **bigger**, so you multiply. Converting up to a larger unit makes the number smaller, so you divide. Prefixes you must know are **centi (10⁻²), milli (10⁻³), micro (10⁻⁶) and nano (10⁻⁹)**.

bullets: 2 µm = 2 × 10⁻⁶ m (move the decimal six places).
To compare sizes, **divide the larger by the smaller**: 25 µm ÷ 2.5 µm = 10, so **one order of magnitude**.
Round the ratio to the **nearest power of ten** to state the order of magnitude.
Use your calculator’s **EXP or ×10ⁿ** button correctly, and write the final answer in **standard form** if asked.
Always include the **unit** with your answer.
core.h: Standard form and order of magnitude (Higher tier)
core.p: **Standard form** writes a number as **A × 10ⁿ**, where A is at least 1 and less than 10 and n is a whole number. Very small sizes such as cells are written with a **negative power of ten**. An **order of magnitude** is a power of ten: if one thing is about 10 times bigger than another, it is **one order of magnitude** bigger; 100 times bigger is **two orders of magnitude**. These skills let you compare cells of very different sizes sensibly.

bullets: **Mitochondria** (aerobic respiration) are found in **eukaryotic** cells, not in bacteria.
**Chloroplasts** (photosynthesis) are found in **plant** cells and some algae, not in bacteria or animal cells.
**Ribosomes** are found in **both** types of cell, where they make proteins.
**Cell membrane** and **cytoplasm** are found in **all** cells.
**Cell wall**: found in bacteria and plant cells, not animal cells. The plant wall is **cellulose**.
**Flagella** are found in some bacteria for movement.
**Permanent vacuole** with cell sap: plant cells only.
core.p: Beyond the headline difference, prokaryotes and eukaryotes differ in other structures, which are often tested in diagram questions. A bacterial cell is drawn with a cell wall and a loop of DNA, with very little else inside. A eukaryotic cell contains many organelles such as the nucleus and mitochondria. The more complex structure of eukaryotic cells allows them to carry out many different jobs, which is why they can form specialised tissues.

bullets: Binary fission is **simple cell division** in bacteria.
One bacterium → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16: the number **doubles** each division.
Number of bacteria after n divisions = **2ⁿ** (starting from one).
In 2 hours at one division per 20 minutes there are 6 divisions: 2⁶ = **64** bacteria.
Rate depends on **nutrients, temperature and oxygen** (link to culturing microorganisms).
Eukaryotic body cells divide by **mitosis** instead (see the cell cycle notes).
Fast reproduction helps antibiotic resistance spread by natural selection.
core.p: Prokaryotes such as bacteria reproduce by **binary fission**, a form of simple cell division where one cell splits into two. The DNA loop and any plasmids are copied first, then the cell divides so that each new cell receives a copy. In ideal conditions (enough nutrients and a suitable temperature) bacteria can divide as often as **once every 20 minutes**, so their numbers rise **exponentially**. This explains why an infection can take hold so fast.

bullets: **Microscopy**: bacteria are near the limit of the light microscope; plasmids need an electron microscope.
**Culturing microorganisms**: bacteria grow on agar and divide by binary fission.
**Pathogens**: bacteria cause disease by reproducing fast and producing toxins.
**Antibiotics**: kill bacteria but not viruses or your own cells; resistance genes can be on plasmids.
**Genetic engineering**: plasmids are used as vectors, and bacteria make useful proteins such as human insulin.
**Cell division**: eukaryotic cells use mitosis; bacteria use binary fission.
**Specialised cells**: only eukaryotic cells become specialised for different jobs.
core.p: The difference between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells shows up all over the GCSE specification. Whenever you meet bacteria in disease, culturing or genetic engineering, you are using this knowledge. Making these links in extended answers shows depth of understanding and can lift an answer into the top mark band.

bullets: Label lines must **touch the structure** and should not cross each other.
Write **cell membrane**, not just "membrane" if the diagram also has a cell wall.
Draw the **DNA loop as a closed ring**, not as a straight line.
Draw **plasmids as separate small circles**.
Do **not** draw a nucleus in a bacterium.
In an animal cell, draw the nucleus as a **round structure inside the cytoplasm**.
If asked to calculate **actual size** from a drawing, measure carefully with a ruler in mm and convert units (see magnification notes).
core.p: Labelling questions are easy marks if you are systematic. Use a ruler for label lines, make sure each line touches the right structure, and use the exact name from the specification. In a drawing question, draw clear, sharp lines with no shading and keep proportions sensible. A good bacterium diagram has a rod or oval outline with a visible wall and membrane, a loop of DNA, small plasmid rings and no nucleus.

exam: **1 mark (State/Name/Label)**: give the exact spec word, e.g. "plasmid", "nucleus", "cell wall". Do not add extra wrong detail.
**2 marks (Describe a difference)**: make a **comparison with both cell types**, e.g. "eukaryotic cells have a nucleus whereas prokaryotic cells have a single loop of DNA free in the cytoplasm".
**Compare questions**: always use link words such as **"whereas"** or **"but"** so the two sides are in the same sentence; a list of facts about one cell only does not score.
**3 to 4 marks (Identify a cell from a diagram)**: name the type, quote the **evidence** (no nucleus; DNA loop; plasmid), and name the example (bacterium).
**Size comparison**: use **"smaller than"** or **"larger than"**, and quote the figure with the unit.
**Calculations**: show the conversion line, e.g. 2 µm = 2 × 10⁻⁶ m, because there is usually a method mark; give the **unit** in the answer.
**Higher tier**: be ready to give an **order of magnitude** by dividing the larger size by the smaller and rounding to a power of ten.

**6 mark extended answer**: structure it as (1) similarities (membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, DNA), (2) genetic material, (3) size, (4) other structures, (5) a link such as plasmids and antibiotic resistance, and end with a conclusion.
**Command words**: "State" = short fact; "Describe" = say what it is like; "Explain" = give a reason (because); "Compare" = similarities and differences together.
**Data/graph tip**: if given a scale bar or a table of cell sizes, check the **unit column** before comparing numbers.

mistakes.r: They do have DNA: a single loop (and plasmids) that is not enclosed in a nucleus.
mistakes.w: Prokaryotic cells have no DNA / no genetic material.

mistakes.r: The main genetic material is the single DNA loop; plasmids are small extra rings of DNA.
mistakes.w: Plasmids are the main genetic material of a bacterium.

mistakes.r: Bacteria are prokaryotes; their wall is not made of cellulose, and they have no nucleus.
mistakes.w: Bacteria are plant cells because they have a cell wall.

mistakes.r: Animal and plant cells are eukaryotic; only bacteria (prokaryotes) lack a nucleus.
mistakes.w: Animal and plant cells are prokaryotic.

mistakes.r: 1 mm = 1000 µm and 1 µm = 1000 nm: each step is a factor of 1000.
They are smaller and simpler in structure, but they carry out all life processes including respiration, with no mitochondria.
mistakes.w: Prokaryotes are smaller, so they are simple and do not respire.

mistakes.r: Use comparative wording: prokaryotic cells are smaller than eukaryotic cells.
Draw a closed ring of DNA free in the cytoplasm, with plasmids as separate small circles and no nucleus.
mistakes.w: Drawing a nucleus in a bacterium, or drawing the DNA loop as a line.

summary: AQA 4.1.1.1: you must describe and compare eukaryotic cells (cell membrane, cytoplasm and genetic material enclosed in a nucleus; animal and plant cells) with prokaryotic cells (smaller, with a single DNA loop and plasmids but no nucleus; bacteria), and use prefixes and standard form to compare sizes. It underpins microscopy, disease, antibiotic resistance and genetic engineering.

terms.d: A cell with genetic material enclosed in a nucleus; animal and plant cells are eukaryotic.
A smaller cell with genetic material not enclosed in a nucleus; bacteria are prokaryotic.
The structure in a eukaryotic cell that contains the genetic material and controls the activities of the cell.
The structure around the cytoplasm that controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell.
The gel-like substance in a cell where most chemical reactions take place.
A rigid layer outside the cell membrane that strengthens the cell; made of cellulose in plant cells.
A small ring of DNA, found in bacteria, in addition to the main DNA loop.
The main genetic material of a prokaryotic cell, free in the cytoplasm and not enclosed in a nucleus.
A structure in the nucleus made of a long molecule of DNA carrying many genes.
A tiny structure in the cytoplasm where proteins are made (protein synthesis).
A part of a cell with a specific function, such as the nucleus or a mitochondrion.
Simple cell division in bacteria in which one cell divides into two.
A unit of length equal to 1 × 10⁻⁶ m; 1000 µm = 1 mm.
A unit of length equal to 1 × 10⁻⁹ m; 1000 nm = 1 µm.
A way of writing numbers as A × 10ⁿ where 1 ≤ A < 10 and n is a whole number.
A power of ten; a quantity 10 times bigger is one order of magnitude bigger.
A long whip-like structure that some bacteria use to move.

worked.ans: (a) 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ m; (b) 20 times larger; (c) about one order of magnitude.
worked.q: A bacterial cell is 2.0 µm long. An animal cell is 40 µm across. (a) Write the length of the bacterial cell in metres in standard form. (b) How many times larger is the animal cell? (c) State the difference in orders of magnitude. (4 marks)
steps: (b) Divide the larger by the smaller: 40 ÷ 2.0 = 20.
(c) 20 is closest to 10¹ (a factor of about 10 to 100), so the animal cell is roughly **one** order of magnitude larger (more than 10 times, less than 100 times).

worked.ans: Model answer: Prokaryotic cells such as bacteria have no nucleus, whereas eukaryotic cells such as animal and plant cells have their genetic material enclosed in a nucleus. A prokaryote has a single loop of DNA and plasmids free in the cytoplasm, but a eukaryote has its DNA in chromosomes inside the nucleus. Prokaryotic cells are smaller than eukaryotic cells. Both types have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and ribosomes.
worked.q: Compare prokaryotic cells with eukaryotic cells. (4 marks)
steps: Mark 1: prokaryotic cells have no nucleus, whereas eukaryotic cells have genetic material enclosed in a nucleus.
Mark 2: prokaryotic cells have a single DNA loop (and plasmids) in the cytoplasm, whereas eukaryotic cells have chromosomes in the nucleus.
Mark 3: prokaryotic cells are smaller than eukaryotic cells.
Mark 4: both have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and ribosomes (similarity), or eukaryotic cells have mitochondria whereas prokaryotic cells do not.
